query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled pre-oxidation annealing treatment that forms a thin, adherent spinel oxide layer on the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating will improve its high-temperature sliding wear performance by reducing both macroscale wear and microscopic plastic deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating on a conventional metal substrate with its as-deposited microstructure and a native or non‐uniform oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Apply a pre-oxidation treatment by annealing the coating under a controlled oxygen partial pressure to deliberately form a well‐defined, thin spinel oxide layer on the coating surface.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding conditions where thermal activation promotes oxidation and microstructural evolution.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a uniform, adherent thin spinel oxide layer at the coating surface.
generation.mechanism: The protective spinel oxide layer is expected to modify dislocation dynamics and reduce the direct metal-to-metal contact during sliding. This layer acts as a barrier that reduces plastic deformation beneath the surface and limits wear by lowering friction and impeding oxidation-induced degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline, the pre-oxidized coating will exhibit reduced wear rates and less microscopic deformation (e.g., smaller or fewer deformation bands and reduced plastic flow features) under identical high-temperature sliding tests.
generation.baseline: The untreated FeNiCrCoCu coating with its initial microstructure and native, less protective oxide formations.
generation.boundary: This effect is anticipated only under high-temperature sliding conditions where thermal activation supports both the formation of the oxide layer and its influence on deformation mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies suggest that protective oxide layers can improve tribological performance at elevated temperatures, the quantitative reduction in wear rate and the changes in microscopic deformation mechanisms in this specific alloy system are uncertain and require experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coated samples: one set undergoes the controlled pre-oxidation annealing treatment to form the spinel oxide layer, and the other set remains as the baseline. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature reciprocating sliding wear tests under controlled load and temperature. Characterize wear rates using mass loss measurements and microscopic deformation via surface microscopy and cross-sectional electron microscopy.
measurements: Wear rate (mass loss per unit sliding distance)
Microstructural analysis of the worn surfaces (e.g., thickness, continuity of the oxide layer, presence of wear tracks, and signs of plastic deformation)
Phase identification of the oxide and substrate using X-ray diffraction (XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not show a statistically significant decrease in wear rate and microscopic plastic deformation compared to the baseline samples under high-temperature sliding conditions, or if the intended thin, uniform spinel oxide layer is absent despite the treatment, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . decision.trend: Early studies on HEA systems under high-temperature conditions first focused on characterizing how thermally activated processes – such as dynamic recrystallization, phase precipitation, and oxidation-induced phase transformation – affect mechanical responses. Initial work (e.g., PMC7515071) demonstrated that wear behavior can be linked to the formation of protective spinel phases at elevated temperatures, while later efforts (e.g., PMC7304825) involving nanocrystalline coatings showed that controlled annealing and consequent microstructural refinement improve tribological performance. However, these studies generally varied processing parameters or alloy composition without isolating a single, mechanistic handle that directly ties microstructural evolution to the wear and deformation phenomena during sliding.
decision.unsolved: A unified, testable hypothesis that explicitly connects a controlled microstructural change (e.g., formation of a thin, adherent oxide or spinel layer) to directional improvements in wear resistance and microscopic deformation during high-temperature sliding has not yet been established for FeNiCrCoCu coatings. The key challenge is to quantitatively correlate a specific alteration in the coating’s microstructure—achieved through a controlled treatment—with predictable changes in tribological behavior under thermal activation.
decision.lever: Introduce a pre-oxidation treatment by annealing the baseline FeNiCrCoCu coating in a controlled oxygen partial pressure environment to form a well‐defined, thin oxide (spinel) layer
decision.why: This approach directly leverages prior evidence that high-temperature oxidation processes can produce protective phases (as seen in PMC7515071 and PMC7304825) which modify dislocation dynamics and wear behavior. By deliberately controlling the oxidation treatment, the experiment is designed to test whether the formation of a specific oxide scale is the governing mechanism that improves wear resistance and alters microscopic deformation during sliding in the high-temperature regime. A falsifying result would be the absence of any corresponding directional change in wear or deformation despite successful formation of the targeted oxide phase.
